title: fix(commit): collapse and cap the auto-staging untracked listing
body:
#4111 switched the status read behind the auto-staging warning to `-uall`, so the warning sees untracked files that `status.showUntrackedFiles=no` hides. That flag also expands every untracked directory into its files, so `wt step commit`, `wt step squash`, and `wt merge` listed 300 paths for a directory of 300 new files before committing.

The warning now reads git's `normal` untracked mode instead. It still overrides `status.showUntrackedFiles=no`, but names a wholly untracked directory once as `dir/`, so a directory of generated files takes one row and can't push a separate new file out of view. The file count stays visible in the commit progress line that follows.

The listing also stops at ten rows. Past ten paths it lists nine and a hint counts the rest, so the hint always stands for at least two paths:

```
▲ Auto-staging 11 untracked paths:
   ┃ 0-generated/
   ┃ 01.txt
   ┃ …
   ┃ 08.txt
↳ … and 2 other paths
◎ Generating commit message and committing changes... (310 files)
```

The status read also moves into the warning itself. Commit and squash each built that command before calling the warning, one through `WorkingTree` and one through `Repository`; both now go through the `WorkingTree` they stage.

Thanks to @Duang777, whose #4112 proposed the cap. They're credited as co-author.

title: fix(config): keep hook pipelines' spelling and comments on save; expand ~ in PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR
body:
Two small fixes found while reviewing v0.78.0.

**A config save rewrote hook pipelines into another spelling, dropping their comments.** A pipeline serializes in one spelling whatever the file used: one step as its lone table, more as an inline array of tables. So every user-config save (declining the commit-generation offer, say) found an untouched pipeline "changed" and rewrote it:

- `[[post-start]]` blocks — the documented form — lost the comment above them; a one-step pipeline became `[post-start]`, and a longer one collapsed into an inline array moved to the top of the file.
- `post-start = [{ … }]` became a `[post-start]` table with the comment above it rendered inside the brackets. Since #4140 the save refuses to write TOML it can't read back, and prompts whose decline path ignores the save error came back on every run.

`merge_tables` now re-spells the desired pipeline the way the file writes it (`in_existing_spelling`) before comparing, and merges `[[…]]` blocks block by block. An untouched pipeline stays byte-identical; a step the load rewrote (template migration renaming `repo_root`) changes alone, keeping its trailing comment. `test_saving_config_mutation_keeps_each_pipeline_spelling_and_its_comments` covers the inline array, one `[[post-switch]]` block, and two `[[pre-start]]` blocks; it fails without the change.

**`wt config plugins pi install` ignored `~` in `$PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`.** Pi expands a leading `~` there (`getAgentDir` → `normalizePath`), so a quoted `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR="~/x"` means a directory under home; wt created a literal `~` directory under the cwd. `pi_agent_dir` now uses `worktrunk::path::expand_tilde`, and `test_pi_install_honors_agent_dir_override` covers the `~/…` case. `omp.rs` is unchanged: oh-my-pi resolves the same variable with a plain `path.resolve`.

title: docs(tend): hold PRs that can make wt delete more, not ones that edit deletion code
body:
The data-loss hold in the tend review reference fired on proximity: a diff that edited a file containing a deletion command, or code near the force-delete path, was held for human review. That held #4146, which made the branch-deletion check stricter and which the reviewer itself called safer than what it replaced.

The hold now fires on what a diff can do: make worktrunk destroy something it used to keep, by adding a deletion, widening what an existing one can delete, or loosening a check that gates one (the dirty-worktree check, the integration check behind `wt remove`'s branch deletion). The command list stays as examples of where deletions live, a held review names how the diff could make a deletion destroy more, and the regenerable / throwaway-environment bound is unchanged.

| Case | Expected | Old | New |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stricter `has_added_changes_by_sha` (the #4146 change) | approve | 0/3 | 3/3 |
| Patch-id fix that stops a false squash-merge match | approve | 0/3 | 3/3 |
| Reworded `wt remove -D` warning in a file calling `remove_dir_all` | approve | 0/3 | 3/3 |
| Trash-sweep threshold one day → seven days | approve | — | 3/3 |
| Dirty check swapped to a command that misses untracked files | hold | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| Squash-merge match loosened to "same file paths" | hold | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| `git worktree remove --force --force` for locked worktrees | hold | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| `rename_into_trash` moved above `ensure_clean` | hold | — | 7/7 |
| `wt step prune` path taken from the rendered `worktree-path` template | hold | — | 7/7 |

The last two include four runs each of a variant that leaves the consequence out of the case. A third arm without a "code on the deletion path gets an ordinary review" sentence scored the same, so that sentence was cut. worktrunk-bot's suggested fourth trigger ("changes what an existing deletion targets or when it fires relative to its gate") held the reorder and retarget cases 3/3 too, and held the narrowing patch-id fix in 1 of 3 runs.

title: fix(git): run diffs through plumbing so user git config can't change what wt reads
body:
Porcelain `git diff` reads display configuration that changes what it reports, and `wt` parsed its output. With `diff.relative = true`, `wt remove <branch>` run from a subdirectory deleted an unmerged branch whose changes sat outside that directory, reporting "no added changes". `color.ui = always` and `diff.external` put escape codes or an external tool's output into the commit, squash, and summary prompts.

Every diff `wt` parses, counts, caches, renders, or sends to an LLM now runs `diff-tree`, `diff-index`, or `diff-files`, which ignore that configuration. This follows the plumbing question raised in the review of #4112.

## Where to look

- `src/git/repository/diff.rs`: `PreparedDiff` is the one path for rendered and prompted diffs, with working-tree, staged, and commit-pair sides read from the real index or a borrowed `TempIndex`. It restores the `git diff` defaults plumbing lacks (rename detection, textconv, hidden intent-to-add entries), overrides `submodule.<name>.ignore` (which plumbing still honors), names the output format, and ends revisions with `--`. `DIFF_PREFIX_OVERRIDES` is gone.
- `src/git/repository/integration.rs`: `has_added_changes_by_sha` runs `diff-tree --quiet --ignore-submodules=none`, and both sides of the patch-id squash-merge check pass `--ignore-submodules=none` too. `BranchDiffSpec` carries a resolved `diff_base`, since `diff-tree` has no three-dot form and `--merge-base` refuses several merge bases. The empty tree follows the repository's object format, so a SHA-256 repository can make its first commit.
- `HEAD±`, `main…±`, `changed_files`, `unmerged_paths`, the picker's per-commit log stats, and the commit, squash, and merge diffstats read plumbing too, all with `--ignore-submodules=none`. `main…±` sparse pathspecs now resolve from the repository root.

Two related fixes where user config meets the commands that write:

- `wt merge --no-ff` builds its merge commit with `commit-tree`, which ignores `commit.gpgSign`; it now passes `--gpg-sign` when that setting is on.
- `wt step rebase` and `wt merge` pass `--no-update-refs`, so `rebase.updateRefs` can't move other branches stacked in the rebased range.

`wt step diff` stays porcelain (`TempIndex::stream_diff`), because it shows the user git's own view. `has_staged_changes` and the `git status` checks are untouched, since #4112 rewrites them.

## Behavior users can see

Picker diff previews, LLM summaries, and prompts no longer follow `diff.external`, `diff.noprefix`, or `color.ui = always`. `main…±` detects renames whatever `diff.renames` says.

## Testing

New tests cover branch deletion under `diff.relative`, a submodule bump under `submodule.<name>.ignore = all` (including a squash merge that dropped or carried the bump), prompts under hostile diff config, a `main/` directory beside the `main` target, criss-cross merge bases, intent-to-add entries and renames in the fallback commit message, a SHA-256 first commit, sparse checkout from a subdirectory, a signed `

title: fix(config): report ignored project-config keys from every worktree
body:
## Problem

`ProjectConfig::load` gated its unknown-field warning on `is_main_worktree`, so
the "key … will be ignored" message never fired outside the primary worktree.
`wt merge` runs from the feature worktree, which is why the issue reads as a
`wt merge` gap — but the suppression is the load path, not the command. `wt
list`, `wt switch`, and every other command are equally silent there:

```
$ cd repo.feat && wt list         # .config/wt.toml has [merge]
(nothing)
$ cd repo && wt list
▲ Project config has unknown field … (will be ignored)
```

`wt config show` warns from anywhere because it renders the same warnings
through its own path (`collect_unknown_warnings`), which has no such gate. A
bare repo, where every worktree is linked, never saw the warning at all.

The consequence the issue describes follows from that: a project `[merge]`
section is dropped at runtime with nothing said, so a machine carrying the
`[projects."<id>"]` entry in user config merges one way and a fresh checkout of
the same repo merges the other.

## Solution

Drop the gate. The warning's fix — edit the tracked `.config/wt.toml`, or move
the key into user config — is available from any worktree, so "only in main
worktree where it's actionable" (#758) doesn't hold for this channel.

The adjacent deprecation channel keeps its gate. That one's message points at
`wt config update`, which does need the primary worktree, and
`format_deprecation_details` already has separate linked-worktree handling for
it. Emission stays deduped per path per process and still respects
`suppress_warnings()`, so the picker and `wt list statusline` are unaffected.

## Testing

`test_misplaced_project_key_warns_from_linked_worktree` writes `[merge]` into a
linked worktree's project config and asserts the warning on `wt list` there. It
fails on `main` ("got: ○ Showing 5 worktrees…") and passes with the change. It
sits beside `test_unknown_project_key_warning_during_load`, its primary-worktree
counterpart.

The issue's own repro now warns before merging:

```
$ wt -C ../repro.feat merge --no-remove
▲ Project config has key merge which belongs in user config (will be ignored); to scope it to this repo, add it under [projects."<id>"] in user config
◎ Merging 1 commit to main @ 1552839 …
```

`cargo test --test integration` is green (2181 passed) apart from two
`step_copy_ignored` cases that also fail on an unmodified tree in this sandbox
— `AF_UNIX` bind is blocked and the umask is 0002. Same for
`copy::tests::test_copy_dir_recursive_does_not_count_a_non_regular_file` under
`--lib`. `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets` are clean.

Closes #4144 — automated triage

title: refactor(config): migrate template variables through MiniJinja's own parser
body:
## Problem

Follow-up to @max-sixty's question on #4124: *"Do we need our own minijinja hand-rolled scanner?"*

No. `src/config/deprecation.rs` located the identifiers it migrates with a scanner that re-derived MiniJinja's grammar from the raw string — where a tag ends, how whitespace control is spelled, what a quoted string is, what `{% raw %}` makes literal, and how `set`/`for`/`with` target lists are shaped. Every place that second reading disagreed with the parser was visible in the file worktrunk writes: #4117 was a `}}` inside a string ending a tag early, and the two review rounds on #4124 added parenthesized tuple targets, `+` whitespace control, and tags inside `{% raw %}`. Each fix made the scanner longer and the next disagreement harder to rule out, because nothing structurally tied it to what MiniJinja actually does.

## Solution

Enable MiniJinja's `unstable_machinery` and parse the template instead of scanning it.

`TemplateVars` walks the AST once and collects two things: the reads, which are the `Expr::Var` nodes — by construction the set the renderer resolves against the context — and the bound names, which are the statements' own target expressions. The rewrite then splices at the byte ranges the parser gave those nodes. Everything the scanner had to decide for itself is now the parser's answer: quoted delimiters, whitespace control, comments, `{% raw %}` contents, attribute names, keyword-argument names, nested tuple targets.

That deletes seventeen functions — the tag walker, the target-list reader with its `TargetsEndAt` modes, the quote and identifier scanners, the `{% raw %}` state machine — for nine short visitor methods. It also collapses detection and migration into one call (`migrate_retired_vars`) instead of two functions sharing a predicate, so the framework invariant is now structural rather than maintained.

The shadowing policy is unchanged: a retired or canonical name bound anywhere still drops the whole pair rather than renaming per scope. The AST would now support real scope tracking, but that is a behavior change, not a simplification, so it stays out of this PR.

## What this costs

Two things worth weighing against the deletion, both stated up front:

- **`unstable_machinery` has no semver guarantee.** MiniJinja last changed it in a *patch* release (1.0.16 moved `tokenize`/`parse` signatures), so a version bound wouldn't reliably prevent a break. The coupling here is to the AST's shape alone and both matches are exhaustive, so the failure mode is a compile error naming the node to handle — never a silent mis-migration. CI catches it on a bump; a `cargo install` against a future MiniJinja would fail to build rather than misbehave.
- **~116KB of release binary** (~67KB stripped), measured by building both ways. `unstable_machinery` pulls in `internal_debug`, which derives `Debug` across the AST and instruction types. The `Cargo.toml` comment now records this against the ~200KB the trimmed feature set saves.

title: fix(config): refuse to write a config rewrite that is not valid TOML
body:
A config rewrite that breaks the TOML syntax leaves a file wt can't load: every later command skips user config with a warning, and commands that need project config fail, until the user hand-edits it. #4120 fixed one such rewrite (an inline table converted to `[# comment\nmerge ]`); this makes the next one fail instead of writing.

`ensure_config_parses` (`src/config/mod.rs`) parses the content before it's persisted, in both writers that rewrite a config file the user owns:

- `UserConfig::save_to` checks just before `write_atomically`.
- `wt config update` checks when it computes the migration (`UpdateCandidate::new`, which also replaces the two duplicated struct literals). The in-place update and `--output` both refuse it there, before the preview prompt.

On refusal the file on disk is unchanged. No rewrite produces invalid TOML today, so the error paths have no integration trigger; a unit test covers the check against the #4120 output shape.

title: docs(config): correct two docstrings naming retired template variables
body:
Requested by @max-sixty in https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/issues/2984#issuecomment-5701831694 — "fix those references, add a TODO to remove the vars in 3 months".

#4080 stopped supplying the retired template variables to any renderer and moved their renames into the load-path deprecation layer. Two docstrings still described the old behavior, and there was no record of when the rename rows themselves can go.

## Comment fixes

- `format_path`'s argument doc said `main_worktree` "supplies both `{{ main_worktree }}` and `{{ repo }}`". #4080 deleted the `vars.insert("main_worktree", …)` line directly below it, so only `{{ repo }}` is supplied now.
- `Command::template`'s doc offered `{{ worktree }}` as an example variable; it is retired to `worktree_path`.

## TODO on `RETIRED_VARS`

Dates the removal at 2026-12-16, three months on from #4080, and records the constraint that makes the rows non-uniform: dropping a row stops the rename, so the old name has to fail loudly on its own first. A hook, alias, or `worktree-path` template already does, through `SemiStrict` expansion — but `commits` renders under minijinja's `Lenient`, which iterates an undefined value as an empty sequence, so dropping that row alone would silently empty a squash prompt's commit list. That row can only go once `build_prompt` rejects the name itself, which is the open question on #2984.

Comments only — no behavior change, no `CHANGELOG.md` entry. `cargo clippy --lib --all-features`, `cargo fmt --check`, and `cargo test --lib config::` (550 tests) pass locally.

body:
Version bump to 0.78.0 plus the changelog section for this release, a comment-preservation fix the release review turned up, a PTY test-filter fix, and merges of `main` (commits that landed during the review, including #4124, #4122, #4141, #4140 and #4145).

**Bump level**: minor. `cargo semver-checks` reports 2 breaking library changes — a new `leftover_branch` field on the `GitError::WorktreeCreationFailed` struct variant, and `DEPRECATED_TEMPLATE_VARS` removed. Pre-1.0, so a breaking change takes a minor bump.

A config save — declining the commit-generation offer, say — dropped the trailing comment on every value it rewrote. That was already true in v0.77.0 for a line the save itself changed (`skip-commit-generation-prompt = false  # note` → `true`, reproduced on the v0.77.0 binary). #4080 widened it to lines the command never touched: retired template variables now migrate on every load, so the next unrelated save rewrote any line naming one. #4080's own PR said this "needs a call before merge" and merged without one.

title: Add repo guidance: delegate other tools' rules, and don't defend improbable environments
body:
Four times in the last 24 hours, `max-sixty` asked a bot PR for less code, and
each time the ask was the same one in a different costume: stop encoding
another tool's rules in `wt`, and stop defending environments that are already
broken. Nothing in `CLAUDE.md` said either, so each PR re-learned it in review.
The first extends **Code Quality → Use Existing Dependencies**, which already
tells you to reach for a dependency before hand-rolling a utility; the second
gets its own heading beside it, since defending an environment has nothing to
do with dependencies.

Both cases the delegation rule came from resolved *into* its exception rather
than out of it — #4085 established that zsh has no "where should the config
file go" to ask, and #4124 that MiniJinja exposes no binding list without
`unstable_machinery`. The guidance names neither: cited as examples, they read
as debt still to pay off, and the zsh decision already lives in
`zsh_config_dir`'s docstring, which is where the rule says that reasoning
belongs.

The generalisation is the maintainer's, not an inference from the diffs —
on #4085: *"can we try to remove as much as possible from our code that
attempts to interpret the internals of other libraries?"*, prefaced with
*"we hit this on some of the sibling issues"*. #4106 is the standing backlog
that same instinct produced.

**Second half, the anxiety one.** On #4104: *"this is totally fine; we're an
order of magnitude too anxious here. if someone doesn't have a resolvable home
dir, then honoring the xdg config in worktrunk is the least of their
problems"* — the wording here is close to his deliberately. The earlier
instance is #4107, where a bot self-review invented a scan of a stranded fish
config directory and he cut it: *"if someone moves the config dir, then we'll
miss the uninstall, that's fine"*. The **Data Safety** carve-out is explicit
because that section rules the opposite way on purpose, and this paragraph
must not be read as licensing a silent loss.

**Why now rather than at the next instance.** The behaviour is stochastic, so
it carries a 5-occurrence floor; the window took it to six (#4085, #4104,
#4123, #4124 here, plus #4104's `nu-config` round and #4107 recorded on
2026-09-15 in #3980). The bot also has seven PRs open, over the self-initiated
budget — this one is filed anyway because the cost class is a wrong outward
action, not compute: #4124 shipped a hand-rolled MiniJinja binding scanner
whose correctness gap the maintainer had to find himself.

<details><summary>The four corrections, and what each one cost</summary>

| PR | Correction | Outcome |
|----|-----------|---------|
| [#4085](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/pull/4085) | "can we just ask `zsh` for whether the config file should go?" | Bot showed the `zsh -f -c` probe relocates the rule rather than removing it, deleted the zsh-source docstring, and gave `zsh_config_dir` the absolute-only guard the module already applied to `$XDG_DATA_HOME`. The rule itself st
author: worktrunk-bot
diff:
--- CLAUDE.md (+17/-0)
@@ -181,6 +181,23 @@ Check `Cargo.toml` before hand-rolling a utility:
 | ANSI colors | `color_print::cformat!()` | raw escape codes |
 | Template var detection | `minijinja::undeclared_variables(false)` | regex/substring on `{{ var }}` |
 
+Delegation extends past utilities to **another tool's own rules** — where zsh
+reads its config, which TOML keys a schema accepts, how MiniJinja scopes a
+template binding. Ask the library; don't re-derive its rule inside `wt`. A
+re-derived rule is correct on the cases that motivated it and drifts silently
+afterwards. Where the library exposes no API that answers the question, keep
+the substitute no larger than the question and say in the code why it exists.
+
+### Don't Defend Improbable Environments
+
+No resolvable home directory, a config directory the user moved out from under
+the tool that owns it — `wt`'s behavior there is the least of that user's
+problems. Take the working environment as a precondition and drop the fallback
+chain rather than carrying code that is maintained forever and exercised by
+nobody. Dropping a fallback still means failing with an error, never
+`.expect()` — see **Error Handling**. Data safety is the exception, and it has
+its own section.
+
 ### Other
 
 - **Don't suppress warnings** with `#[allow(dead_code)]` — delete the code or add `// TODO(topic): used by <upcoming work>`.

title: test(pty): keep the shell's failed-setpgid diagnostic out of PTY snapshots
body:
`test (macos)` failed on `main` at 41af9ba8cc3e7fffad44da123cb8b5c5f278146d ([run 35065804093](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/actions/runs/35065804093)) with one snapshot mismatch in `integration_tests::shell_wrapper::unix_tests::test_readme_example_switch_back`: a line the shell wrote about its own job-control bookkeeping had landed in the captured PTY output.

```
   1     1 │
         2 │+bash: child setpgid (42242 to 42242): Operation not permitted
   2     3 │ ␛[2m○␛[22m Switched to worktree for ␛[1mfeature-api␛[22m @ ␛[1m_REPO_.feature-api␛[22m␊
```

The line is bash's, not wt's. `exec_in_pty_shell` runs the wrapper tests under `bash -i`, which turns job control on so the suite can catch leaked job notifications, and the bash arm of `build_shell_script` folds stderr into stdout (`exec 2>&1`) so those leaks are visible to the assertions. An interactive bash puts each child it forks into its own process group; when that `setpgid` loses its race against the child's own `setpgid`/exec it prints this diagnostic and carries on. Whether the race is lost is up to host scheduling, so the line shows up in an occasional run and in none of the others — the same test passed on the preceding and following runs of the same workflow on `main`, on the same code path, and the offending output is not something `wt` produced.

So this is a snapshot-normalization gap rather than a behavior change: the capture is meant to hold what a user would see from `wt`, and it is already filtered for host-dependent PTY artifacts (`add_pty_filters` strips the `^D` + backspace sequence macOS PTYs emit at EOF and Linux ones don't). This adds the shell's failed-`setpgid` diagnostic to the same place, so every PTY snapshot test gets it rather than the one test that happened to catch it.

The filter is deliberately narrow. Job-control *notifications* — `[1] 12345` and `[1]+ Done`, the leaks `assert_no_job_control_messages` and `test_bash_job_control_suppression` exist to catch — do not match it and stay in the output; the new test in [`tests/common/mod.rs`](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/83bf42c33a954cf9c326bd42cb0c2a497d7140ab/tests/common/mod.rs) pins both halves by running a capture containing all three lines through the filters and snapshotting what survives.

title: feat(config)!: split the Pi and oh-my-pi plugin installers
body:
`wt config plugins pi` installed an oh-my-pi hook. It wrote a `HookAPI` module to `~/.omp/agent/hooks/pre/worktrunk.ts` and read `$PI_CONFIG_DIR` / `$OMP_PROFILE` / `$PI_PROFILE` — all oh-my-pi's. Pi (earendil-works/pi) loads `ExtensionAPI` extensions from `~/.pi/agent/extensions/`, so a Pi user who ran that command got a file Pi never reads, and `wt config show` printed a PI section off `which omp`.

This splits them into two commands, because they are two agents:

| | `wt config plugins omp` | `wt config plugins pi` |
|---|---|---|
| Writes | `~/.omp/agent/hooks/pre/worktrunk.ts` | `~/.pi/agent/extensions/worktrunk.ts` |
| Source | `dev/omp-hook.ts` (`HookAPI`) | `dev/pi-extension.ts` (`ExtensionAPI`) |
| Config roots | `$PI_CONFIG_DIR`, `$OMP_PROFILE`/`$PI_PROFILE`, `$PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` | `$PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` |
| Detected by | `which omp` | `which pi` |

`wt config show` now renders PI and OH-MY-PI as separate sections, each gated on its own binary.

## The `pi` rename is the breaking part

`wt config plugins pi install` has meant oh-my-pi since 0.77.0, and it now means Pi. Already-installed hooks keep working — the path is unchanged — so what breaks is the command name in scripts and dotfiles. Both halves of that now say so rather than failing quietly:

- **`pi install`** would write a Pi extension for someone who has only oh-my-pi, and nothing downstream would mention it: the PI section of `wt config show` is gated on `which pi`, which they don't have. It now warns before writing — `▲ oh-my-pi is on PATH and Pi is not; for the oh-my-pi hook, run wt config plugins omp install`.
- **`pi uninstall`** would look at `~/.pi/agent/extensions/`, print `Plugin not installed`, and exit 0 — a no-op that reads as a completed removal while the hook sits untouched under `~/.omp/`. It now adds `↳ An oh-my-pi hook is installed; to remove it, run wt config plugins omp uninstall`.

An oh-my-pi user who reruns `pi install` despite the warning is still routed home by `wt config show`: the hook source text changed in the rename, so the byte-compare misses and the OH-MY-PI section prints `Plugin outdated. To update, run wt config plugins omp install`.

**The open decision is whether that's enough, or whether `pi` should warn-and-redirect for one release before it changes meaning.** The flip is what's implemented here; the deprecation is a small change on top if preferred.

## Provenance and verification

The first commit is @ashebanow's, from [`feat/pi-and-omp-plugin-targets`](https://github.com/ashebanow/worktrunk/tree/feat/pi-and-omp-plugin-targets), cherry-picked unmodified — this PR exists because #4133 asked for the implementation and the branch was already there and already verified. @ashebanow, if you'd rather carry this yourself, say so and I'll close it.

That verification is the part CI can't do: the commit message records an end-to-end run against pi 0.85.1 (extension discovered at `~/.pi/agent/extensions/`, `agent_start` → 🤖, `agent_end` → 💬, `ses

+// Worktrunk activity tracking extension for Pi (earendil-works/pi).
+//
+// Tracks agent activity per branch, showing status markers in `wt list`:
+//   🤖 — agent is working
+//   💬 — agent is waiting for input
+//
+// Installed globally via: wt config plugins pi install
+//
+// Pi loads user extensions from `~/.pi/agent/extensions/*.ts` (or
+// `$PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR/extensions/`) and hands each factory an
+// `ExtensionAPI`. oh-my-pi is a different agent with a different loader and
+// API — see `dev/omp-hook.ts` and `wt config plugins omp install`.
+
+import type { ExtensionAPI } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent";
+
+export default function worktrunkActivity(pi: ExtensionAPI): void {
+  const run = async (
+    cwd: string,
+    args: ["set", string] | ["clear"],
+  ): Promise<void> => {
+    try {
+      await pi.exec("wt", ["config", "state", "marker", ...args], { cwd });
+    } catch {
+      // Activity tracking must never interrupt the host Pi session.
+    }
+  };
+
+  pi.on("agent_start", async (_event, ctx) => {
+    await run(ctx.cwd, ["set", "🤖"]);
+  });
+
+  // `agent_end` is not the end: Pi may auto-retry, auto-compact and retry, or
+  // pick up a queued follow-up message. `agent_settled` is the event Pi
+  // documents for status integrations — it fires once Pi will not continue
+  // running on its own.
+  pi.on("agent_settled", async (_event, ctx) => {
+    await run(ctx.cwd, ["set", "💬"]);
+  });
+
+  pi.on("session_shutdown", async (_event, ctx) => {
+    await run(ctx.cwd, ["clear"]);
+  });
+}

title: chore: update tend workflows (0.2.7 → 0.2.8)
body:
Regenerates the `tend-*` workflows with tend 0.2.8 (from 0.2.7).

## What changes for this repo

**Pausing tend moves to a repository variable.** Every generated job now gates on
`vars.TEND_ENABLED != 'false'` in its `if:`, replacing the per-job "Check whether
tend is enabled" step that fetched `.config/tend.yaml` over the API and parsed it
with ~70 lines of inlined Ruby. That step is deleted from all nine workflows —
most of the 821 deleted lines here — and every downstream
`if: steps.tend_enabled.outputs.enabled == 'true'` guard goes with it. To pause
tend from now on, set a `TEND_ENABLED` repository variable to `false`; the
`enabled:` config key is no longer the switch. This repo's `.config/tend.yaml`
never set `enabled:`, so nothing here changes behavior — the workflows just get
one fewer API call and Ruby invocation per job.

**Review events get their own relay workflow.** The secretless `relay` job that
re-entered `pull_request_review` / `pull_request_review_comment` events as a
`repository_dispatch` moves out of `tend-mention.yaml` into a new
`tend-mention-relay.yaml`. `tend-mention.yaml` keeps only the
`repository_dispatch` entry point, so its `React with eyes` target now reads
`client_payload.id` unconditionally rather than falling back to a direct event's
`comment.id`. Same path end to end; the split just stops the relay's permissions
and triggers from sharing a file with the secret-bearing jobs.

**Conflict resolution on bot PRs merges the fetched base branch** rather than the
PR's recorded `baseRefOid`, so a base that advanced between the PR read and the
merge no longer leaves the branch conflicting again immediately after a
"resolved" push (max-sixty/tend#1232). This is the machinery that runs against
the bot's own open PRs here.

**uv is invoked by path.** `astral-sh/setup-uv` goes to v10.1.0 with
`UV_NO_MODIFY_PATH: "1"` and `enable-cache: false`, and the verify step calls
`$TEND_UV` (the action's `uv-path` output) instead of a bare `uv`, so the setup
no longer edits the runner's PATH or seeds a cache the job doesn't reuse. Pinned
uv moves 0.12.10 → 0.12.13.

Smaller behavior fixes that ride along: the notifications poll counts queued runs
when deciding whether another run already owns a subject
(max-sixty/tend#1235), `review-runs` no longer treats a generated red run as
live work when a later green run of the same name exists
(max-sixty/tend#1247), and the skills' dedup listings raise their caps to 200
(max-sixty/tend#1239).

Upstream comparison: https://github.com/max-sixty/tend/compare/0.2.7...0.2.8

No model pins in `.config/tend.yaml` to re-check, and the config itself is
unchanged — this PR touches only the generated workflow files.

+# Generated by tend 0.2.8. Regenerate with: uvx tend@latest init
+#
+# Do not edit this file directly — it will be overwritten on regeneration.
+# To customize behavior, edit the relevant skill (for example,
+# `running-tend`) in this repo's .claude/skills/ directory, or open an issue at
+# https://github.com/max-sixty/tend/issues for changes that need to
+# happen upstream in the tend-ci-runner plugin.
+
+name: tend-mention-relay
+# Review events for tend-mention. Their runs carry `refs/pull/N/merge`, which
+# the operational secrets' environment does not admit, so this workflow holds
+# no secret: it re-posts each event as a `repository_dispatch`, which starts
+# tend-mention on the default branch. It is a workflow of its own because
+# GitHub lists every job of a review event's run among the PR's checks, skipped
+# jobs included, so the run holds only the job that can execute. Same-repo PRs
+# only — the notifications poll covers fork PRs.
+on:
+  pull_request_review:
+    types: [submitted]
+  # Not `created`: GitHub also fires `pull_request_review` for every new inline
+  # comment (probed across the comments endpoint, the replies endpoint, the
+  # "Add single comment" button, and reviews submitted with inline comments),
+  # so subscribing would relay each one twice. An edit fires no review event,
+  # so `edited` stays, to catch "@bot" added to an existing comment.
+  pull_request_review_comment:
+    types: [edited]
+
+jobs:
+  # Move the event onto a ref the environment admits, and nothing else. The
+  # merge ref itself can never be admitted — a same-repo `pull_request` run
+  # executes the PR head's own workflow files on that same ref, so admitting
+  # it would hand a pushed workflow the secrets the environment exists to
+  # deny. All judgement lives in tend-mention's `verify`, which re-reads the
+  # review or comment from the API, so a skipped event costs one extra short
+  # run rather than a second copy of the heuristics here.
+  relay:
+    # Fork PRs are excluded to hold long-standing behaviour: the notifications
+    # poll covers them, and it applies author-association tiers that this path
+    # does not. What the filter buys is that no fork head is checked out into a
+    # secret-bearing run; it is not an authorship gate, since a mention from
+    # any user with read access already wakes `handle` on a same-repo PR.
+    # Widening this is a separate decision, and moot while a fork run's token
+    # is refused the dispatch POST (403, probed).
+    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
+    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
+    # No secrets here. `contents: write` is what the dispatch POST needs, and
+    # is the whole of what this token can do — probed both ways on a live
+    # repo: an otherwise identical same-repo run declaring `contents: read`
+    # is refused with 403, so a narrower token would leave every review
+    # mention unanswered rather than merely unprivileged. It grants nobody a
+    # new capability: only someone who can already push a branch can open the
+    # same-repo PR whose workflow file this is, and they could declare any
+    # permissions they liked in it. The merge restriction is what bounds that,
+    # here as everywhere.
+    permissions:
+      contents: write
+    steps:
+      # Identifiers only: `verify` re-reads the review or comment from the
+      # API, so the words the bot weighs and acts on are the ones GitHub
+      # holds, and a forged dispatch faces the same scrutiny as a relayed one.
+      - name: Re-enter on an admitted ref
+        env:
+          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
+        run: |
+          gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/dispatches" \
+            -f event_type=tend-mention-review \
+            -f "client_payload[kind]=${{ github.event_name }}" \
+            -f "client_payload[pr]=${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}" \
+            -f "client_payload[id]=${{ github.event.review.id || github.event.comment.id }}"

title: fix(flake): use stdenv.hostPlatform.isDarwin in commonArgs
body:
Fixes #4131.

`pkgs.stdenv.isDarwin` is a deprecated alias in nixpkgs: it is defined as `lib.warn "stdenv.isDarwin is deprecated, use stdenv.hostPlatform.isDarwin instead"` wrapping the real value (`pkgs/stdenv/generic/default.nix`, added 2026-05-09). Reading it emits that warning on every evaluation of this flake, so downstream consumers see it on every `nix develop`, and it becomes a hard error once nixpkgs drops the alias.

`stdenv.hostPlatform.isDarwin` is the identical boolean, so `libiconv` is still selected on Darwin and the build inputs are unchanged. `flake.nix:245` already uses `pkgs.stdenv.hostPlatform.system`, as does `nix/home-manager-module.nix`, so this makes the file consistent with its own convention.

Verified with `nix flake check` (all outputs evaluate); the warning is gone from an evaluating consumer. No behavior change.

title: Write changelog entries at release time, and tighten the Unreleased entries
body:
Changelog entries written in feature and fix PRs have been running long: the `## Unreleased` section averaged 84 words per entry against the release skill's 35-word target, and entries in open PRs average about 140. The length guidance lives only in `.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md`, which loads at release time, so PR authors never see it and calibrate against the neighbouring entries instead.

- **CLAUDE.md** — `## Releases` now says the release skill writes every changelog entry from the commits since the last tag, so other PRs leave `CHANGELOG.md` untouched, and a PR that already carries an entry drops it rather than resolving a conflict on it. That second clause gives the automated conflict resolver an answer for the PRs already open, which would otherwise re-add their entries here. Tend's review already checks PRs against CLAUDE.md. The release skill's changelog section now opens with drafting entries rather than checking for missing ones.
- **CHANGELOG.md** — the `## Unreleased` entries, including those that landed on `main` while this was open, are rewritten to the skill's ceiling: 18 entries averaging 42 words. Missing PR links are added and the two plugin-status entries are merged. Released sections are untouched.

> _This was written by Claude Code on behalf of max-sixty_

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix(opencode): clear the activity marker when OpenCode 1 disposes the plugin
body:
## Problem

On OpenCode 1.x the plugin's `server` export drives the marker, and its only clearing path is the `session.deleted` event — which fires when a session is explicitly deleted, not when one ends normally. So a finished session leaves its last `set 💬` in place and `wt list` keeps showing a dead session as active until `wt config state marker clear` is run by hand. Reported in #4128 against worktrunk 0.77.0 and OpenCode 1.18.18.

The `server` path does have a teardown hook; the plugin just wasn't implementing it. OpenCode's v1 plugin interface declares [`dispose?: () => Promise<void>`](https://github.com/sst/opencode/blob/v1.18.18/packages/plugin/src/index.ts) as the first member of `Hooks`, and the host calls it from an `Effect.addFinalizer` registered alongside the event subscription in [`packages/opencode/src/plugin/index.ts`](https://github.com/sst/opencode/blob/v1.18.18/packages/opencode/src/plugin/index.ts) — the same place it tears the event listener down. `dispose` has been in that interface since v1.16.0, which is the floor the `server` export already targets, and older hosts ignore an unknown key, so there is no version gate to add.

This also means the issue's suggested route — having OpenCode 1.18 honor `setup()`'s return value as a teardown — is not the path: that loader is the v2 one, and the v1 hook object already carries the teardown.

## Solution

`server()` now returns a `dispose` that clears the marker, mirroring what the OpenCode 2 `setup()` path already does in its returned teardown. The OpenCode 2 path is untouched.

A `dispose` that only calls `clear` isn't enough on its own, because the host dispatches the `event` hook fire-and-forget — `void hook["event"]?.({ event: ... })`, with no `await` and no handle kept. The `wt config state marker set 💬` subprocess spawned by the final `session.idle` is therefore still running when the finalizer calls `dispose`, both write `worktrunk.state.<branch>.marker`, and whichever `wt` finishes last decides it. That gap is narrowest in the issue's own repro: `opencode run "wait"` goes idle and exits immediately.

So every marker call chains onto one promise, which is the handle the `server` path otherwise lacks — the `clear` enqueues behind whatever is outstanding. Effect closes scope finalizers LIFO and the `dispose` finalizer is registered after the one holding `unsubscribe`, so the listener is still live during teardown; a `disposed` flag drops what arrives in that window rather than letting it re-set after the clear.

The doc sentence asserting that every plugin clears on session end was, for this path, false; it is true again with this change. The same sentence still said "all four plugins" while the list above it names five (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Gemini), so that count is corrected in the same edit. The two `claude-code.md` mirrors are the sync test's regeneration of the primary in `docs/src/content/docs/`.

## Testing

Node's type stripping runs `dev/opencode-plugin

title: fix(config): refuse to publish a config migration the preview no longer describes
body:
## Problem

`wt config update` computes each migration before it renders the preview and writes it after the answer. Nothing revisits the file in between, so an edit saved from another terminal while `Apply updates?` is waiting is replaced by the pre-prompt snapshot — and the command reports `✓ Updated user config`, giving no sign that anything was discarded.

The same gap reaches the approvals step: `copy_approved_commands_to_approvals_file` reads the live config after confirmation, while the replacement written a few lines later comes from the earlier candidate, so the two halves of one update can describe different source states.

## Solution

After confirmation and before any mutation, re-read every candidate and compare it against the content its preview was computed from. A config that has moved on fails with its path and a prompt to re-run, leaving the newer file in place:

```
✗ User config changed @ ~/.config/worktrunk/config.toml since the preview; re-run wt config update to migrate the current contents
```

All candidates are verified before any is written, so a superseded user config can't leave the project config half-applied, and the approvals copy now runs against content known to match the candidate. Failing rather than silently re-migrating follows the repository's data-safety rule — a preview authorizes migrating the content it describes, not whatever is on disk when the user answers. `wt config shell uninstall` already takes this position for its own prompt window, where the preview authorizes an exact set of rc lines rather than a rescan.

The window between the final read and the rename stays open to a non-cooperating editor. That is the boundary `CLAUDE.md` already accepts for the shell-config writes, and closing it is not what this change claims.

## Testing

Two PTY cases drive the real prompt and change the file from the prompt callback — the same synchronization `configure_shell.rs` uses for its uninstall race, so there is no sleep or timing assumption. `test_config_update_rejects_preview_stale_at_apply` rewrites the config: before the change the command exits 0, prints `✓ Updated user config`, and the `# preserve this edit` line is gone; after it, the command fails and the file still holds the edit. `test_config_update_rejects_config_removed_at_apply` removes the config instead, the same staleness at its limit, and checks that the file is not recreated from the preview.

The existing accept and decline cases are unchanged, and the 20 non-PTY `config update` cases still pass. None of the four PTY cases in this file — the two new ones and the two pre-existing ones — can run in the CI sandbox: the PTY child is `env_clear`ed, so it inherits no `TMPDIR` and the migration diff's tempdir lands in a read-only `/tmp`. They were verified locally with `TMPDIR` passed through to the child; that harness change is not part of this PR, and CI runs them normally.

Closes #4125 — automated triage

title: fix(config): report a failed migration diff instead of rendering none
body:
## Problem

`format_migration_diff` read only stdout after `Cmd::run()` handed back a
captured `Output`, and a nonzero child status is still `Ok` there. Any
`git diff --no-index` that failed before writing a patch — exit 128, empty
stdout — was therefore indistinguishable from two identical files, so the
`Proposed diff:` block vanished from `wt config show` and from the preview
`wt config update` prompts on, with nothing said about why.

The realistic trigger is the user's own git config. `git diff --no-index`
honors `diff.external`, so a broken, interactive, or GUI diff program
configured for ordinary work was being handed Worktrunk's two temp files.

## Solution

Two changes, both in the renderer:

- Branch on the exit status instead of on stdout: 0 is "identical", 1 is
  "differs", and everything else is a failure carrying git's stderr. The
  helper returns `anyhow::Result<Option<String>>`, which also retires the
  `.expect("git diff --no-index failed")` that would have panicked when git
  could not be spawned at all.
- Pass `--no-ext-diff`, so `diff.external` is never consulted for a patch
  Worktrunk renders for itself.

Both consumers now go through one `format_migration_diff_block`, which
renders the patch, nothing, or a warning with git's stderr in a gutter:

```
▲ Could not render the proposed diff
  git diff --no-index, exit code 128
  error: unknown value for config 'diff.algorithm': bogus
  fatal: unable to parse 'diff.algorithm' from command-line config
```

The preview degrades rather than the command failing, because the migration
itself is computed in memory by `compute_migrated_content` and is unaffected
by the renderer. The deprecation warnings that describe each change still
print, so a user prompted with a degraded preview can see that the patch is
missing and decline.

## Testing

Two integration tests in `tests/integration_tests/config_show.rs`, both
failing before the change:

- `test_config_show_reports_failed_migration_diff` runs `wt config show`
  with `diff.algorithm` set to an unparseable value — a failure that survives
  `--no-ext-diff` — and asserts the warning appears. Before the change the
  command printed the deprecation warning and no diff, exit 0.
- `test_config_show_migration_diff_ignores_external_diff` points
  `diff.external` at a nonexistent program and asserts the patch still
  renders.

Both drive the real binary and set the git config per-child via
`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, so nothing global is touched.

Closes #4118 — automated triage
author: worktrunk-bot

title: fix(config): keep template-variable migration in step with the template parser
body:
## Problem

Deprecated template variables are *found* with MiniJinja (`undeclared_variables`) and *rewritten* with a hand-rolled scanner. The two disagree in two places, and both disagreements are visible in the file worktrunk writes.

**A quoted closing delimiter ended the tag.** `rewrite_template_var_identifiers` located a tag's end with a plain `find("}}")` before handing the body to its quote-aware scanner. On

```jinja
{{ "}} " ~ repo_root }}
```

the tag was cut at the delimiter inside the string, so the real `repo_root` became outside-tag text and no migration happened at all. The mirror case changes output text: in `{{ "}} {{ repo_root }}" }}{{ repo_root }}` the literal `{{ repo_root }}` inside the string was scanned as a tag and rewritten, while the actual reference beside it was not.

**A shadowed name was renamed at every use.** `undeclared_variables` answers whether a name is read before it is bound, not which occurrences are the global one, so

```jinja
{{ repo_root }}{% set repo_root = "local" %}{{ repo_root }}
```

reports `repo_root`, and the scanner — which has no scope tracking — renamed the first *and* the last use. `is_template_attribute_or_assignment` skipped the assignment target only. The final expression then read `repo_path` where the template meant the local.

`test_normalize_skips_set_assignment_target` looked like coverage for the second case, but its name is local throughout, so `undeclared_variables` returns nothing and the scanner never runs.

This matters more than it did: on #4080 this rewrite becomes `Structural`, running on every config load rather than only under `wt config update`.

## Solution

`template_tag_end` scans for the closing delimiter while skipping quoted strings, reusing the existing `quoted_template_string_end`. It replaces the plain `find` for `{{ }}` and `{% %}`. Comments keep the plain scan — MiniJinja does not tokenize strings inside `{# #}`.

For shadowing, the rewriter is not taught scopes; a deprecated name bound anywhere in the template is dropped from the replacement set instead. `template_block_bindings` reads the binding keywords and returns the names they bind. Those are `set`, `for`, and `with`: `Cargo.toml` takes MiniJinja with `default-features = false`, so `macro` and `call` are not statements at all and a template using one fails to parse before the scan runs. A name merely *used* in a block tag — `{% if repo_root %}` — still migrates.

Over-reporting is the safer of the two error directions, but it is not free: because detection reads the same set, a name this scan claims stops warning as well as stops migrating. So the scan is kept as close to MiniJinja's own reading as a scanner can be. Targets are read the way `parse_assignment` reads them, nested parenthesized tuples included; block keywords are split with `+` whitespace control honored alongside `-`; a binding-shaped tag inside `{% raw %}` binds nothing; and a `set`'s targets end at its `=`, since the comma after it builds

title: fix(config): stop reporting valid empty per-project sections as unknown
body:
## Problem

`[projects."example.com/org/repo".list]` is valid config, accepted on load — and every command printed `unknown field projects.example.com/org/repo.list` for it.

A section equal to its default is skipped during serialization, so it is absent from the round-tripped view `diff_tables` compares the raw file against. `seed_schema_skeleton` exists to rescue exactly that, but it restored only *top-level* keys: an emptied `[list]` read as known, the same section one level down read as unknown. All seven `UserProjectOverrides` sections carrying `skip_serializing_if = "is_default"` are affected — `list`, `commit`, `merge`, `remove`, `switch`, `step`, `forge`.

## Solution

`WorktrunkConfig` gains `valid_scoped_keys()` — a top-level key whose entries are themselves schema-typed tables, with the valid keys for one entry. User config returns `("projects", UserProjectOverrides schema keys)`; project config has no such key and keeps the default `None`. `seed_schema_skeleton` applies the same restore inside each entry.

Only schema-valid keys are seeded, so a genuine unknown in that scope still warns. The `UserProjectOverrides` key list has one home — `user_project_override_keys()`, shared with `is_user_project_override_key`.

`remove_section_key_in` in `deprecation.rs` already described this false positive in a comment and worked around it by deleting the section it emptied. That comment is updated to match the fixed behavior; the deletion itself is unchanged.

## Scope after #4160

This PR originally carried a second half, against `UserConfig::save_to`'s `merge_tables` stale-key sweep: `compute_unknown_tree` fed both the warning and the preserve set that a whole-config rewrite consulted, so making a section stop reading as unknown also changed what a save kept. #4160 replaced that rewrite with a single-value edit through `toml_edit` and deleted `save_to` and `merge_tables` outright, so `compute_unknown_tree` now feeds the warning only. Merging `main` dropped that half and its test (`test_save_to_existing_file_keeps_section_holding_only_unknown_keys`, which called the removed `save_to`).

What remains is a warning-path fix with no save-path behavior change. The "empty `[projects."<id>".list]` is now dropped on save" note in the earlier description no longer applies — nothing rewrites the file wholesale for it to apply to.

## Testing

- `empty_per_project_section_is_known` — the reported input produces an empty tree and no warnings. Fails before the change with `NestedUnknown { path: "projects.example.com/org/repo.list" }`.
- `unknown_key_in_per_project_scope_still_warns` — three cases that must keep warning: an unknown sibling section, an unknown key nested inside a known section, and a root-only user setting (`skip-shell-integration-prompt`) that has no per-project form.

`cargo test --lib config::` is 537 passed at the merged head; `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --lib --tests` are clean.

Reported by @zach-hammad-vs from source inspectio

title: fix(config): migrate deprecated keys in an inline [projects] scope
body:
## Problem

`for_each_config_table_mut` — the scope walk behind every per-project deprecation rule — matched only `Item::Table`, for the `projects` container and for each entry inside it. TOML's two equivalent shapes therefore migrated differently:

```toml
[projects."example.com/org/repo".merge]
no-ff = true                                        # migrates to ff = false

[projects]
"example.com/org/repo" = { merge = { no-ff = true } }   # skipped
```

The skipped form is not merely left unmigrated. `UserProjectOverrides`'s `MergeConfig` has `ff` and no `no-ff` alias, so the unmigrated key reaches serde at a path with no field, is dropped from the typed config, and the per-project non-fast-forward merge silently stops applying. An unknown-field warning may fire, but the setting is gone either way.

The rule reached inside an inline `merge = { … }` already — `migrate_negated_bool_inline` exists for exactly that — so the gap was the outer scope, one level up.

## Solution

The walk now visits a `projects` container and a project entry in either shape. An inline entry is migrated through a table view and written back inline, and only when a rule reported a change, so an entry nothing touched keeps its formatting.

This covers every rule on that walk, not just `merge.no-ff`: `switch.no-cd`, the removed `list.task-timeout-ms`, and the `[select]` / `[commit-generation]` section renames. `[ci]` → `[forge]` is not among them — `migrate_ci_doc` reads and writes the document root directly, so it has no per-project scope in either shape.

`rename_hook_key` and `remove_approved_commands_doc` keep their own table-only traversals of `projects` — #4116 flags them as worth an owner-level look. They are left alone here: both move or delete whole items rather than rewriting a key inside a section, so the fix is not the same shape, and folding them into the shared walk is a larger change than this bug needs.

## Testing

- `test_migrate_no_ff_inline_project_scope` — asserts both the migrated text and that the setting reaches the typed config (`config.projects[…].merge.ff == Some(false)`), which is the part that was silently lost.
- `test_migrate_no_ff_fully_inline_projects_table` — the `projects` container itself inline.
- `test_migrate_leaves_unrelated_inline_project_keys_alone` — an entry no rule touched keeps its formatting, and sibling keys in a migrated entry survive the table round-trip.
- `test_warning_fires_iff_update_changes` gains four `rewritten` entries covering the inline scope across `merge.no-ff`, `list.task-timeout-ms`, the `[select]` rename, and `switch.no-cd`, so the framework invariant is checked for the newly-reachable shapes too.

All four fail before the change. `cargo test --lib` passes apart from `copy::tests::test_copy_dir_recursive_does_not_count_a_non_regular_file`, which fails on `main` in this sandbox too (`socket(AF_UNIX, …)` is blocked). `cargo clippy --all-targets` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.

title: fix(config): warn about a deprecated section the migration declined to rewrite
body:
## Problem

`classify_unknown_key` answers `DeprecatedHandled` from the registry alone: the
name is in `DEPRECATED_SECTION_KEYS` and its canonical top-level key is valid
here, so the deprecation channel owns the message. `collect_unknown_warnings`
then skips the key unconditionally.

That holds only when the rewrite actually ran. A migration that *declines* —
`select = "not a table"`, or a `[select]` whose `[switch.picker]` destination is
already occupied — deliberately leaves the key in place and emits no deprecation
warning, because rewriting it would drop the user's value. Both channels then
stay silent, so the setting is read by nobody and reported by no one.

`CLAUDE.md` already specifies the intended handoff: a config that can't be
rewritten safely "is left untouched and unwarned — serde's type or unknown-field
error is the messaging". The unknown-field half of that handoff was suppressed.

## Solution

Treat `DeprecatedHandled` as handled only when migration removed the key. A
deprecated top-level section that survives migration still carrying config falls
through to the ordinary `TopLevelUnknown` warning — no new message shape, just
the one the policy already names.

Two survivors stay silent by design, and the new `deprecated_key_declined`
helper keeps them that way:

- an empty deprecated section, which contributes no config (that is why the
  migration leaves it alone in the first place);
- a *type* error for a known field (`switch = "x"`), where the round-trip
  analysis is `Unreliable` and serde's own message is the diagnostic.

`[ci]` is unaffected: it is still a live `ProjectConfig` field, so its leftover
keys already warn at their own path.

## Testing

`test_unmigrated_deprecated_section_warns_as_unknown` reproduces the report
(`select = "not a table"` yielded zero warnings before the change) and pins the
occupied-destination, malformed-`commit-generation`, empty-section,
type-error, and successfully-migrated cases alongside it.

`test_warning_fires_iff_update_changes` still passes, including its assertion
that what `wt config update` writes raises no unknown-field warning.

Closes #4119 — automated triage

title: fix(config): preserve unknown keys and comments when rewriting an inline config section
body:
## Problem

A config section can be written inline — `merge = { squash = false }` — and worktrunk rewrites the user's config file in two places: `UserConfig::save_to`, and the deprecation migration that runs before serde on every load. Both handled inline sections worse than the `[merge]` spelling, and one of them wrote a file that no longer parsed.

**Unknown keys were dropped on save.** `save_to` preserves schema-unknown keys — a typo, or a field from a newer `wt` — at every nesting level, but only the standard-table branch of `merge_tables` applied that preservation tree. The inline branch compared the existing inline table against the serialized form and, on any difference, replaced the whole item. An unknown key guarantees that difference, so with

```toml
merge = { squash = false, future-option = true }
```

a save triggered by an unrelated setting dropped `future-option`. The same config written as `[merge]` kept it.

**Rewriting an inline section as a standard table produced TOML `wt` can't read.** Both rewrite paths have to convert — the save path once a value inside the section really changed, the migration because TOML forbids extending an inline table with a later subtable — and both left the key's own decor in place. A standard table renders that decor *inside* its brackets, and the key was parsed from `merge = { … }`, so its decor holds everything that preceded the line. A comment, or just a blank line, therefore landed between the brackets:

```toml
# why squash is off
merge = { squash = false }
```

`wt config set merge.squash true` wrote back `[# why squash is off\nmerge ]`, and every later command failed with `TOML parse error at line 2, column 7`. The user's own comment was what broke the file.

The migration path is worse, because it runs on load rather than on save. `commit = { stage = "all" }` under a comment, alongside a deprecated `commit-generation` section — or an inline `switch` alongside `[select]` — stopped the config from loading at all, on every command, at a line number matching nothing the user wrote, and `wt config update` then wrote the broken text to disk.

## Solution

The save path's inline branch now merges into a table view of the existing inline table, recursing through `merge_tables` with that key's `preserve.nested` subtree — the same path the standard-table branch takes. It writes back only when the merge changed something, so an inline section nothing touched keeps its formatting.

When a conversion does happen, it goes through one shared `replace_inline_with_table`: the key's prefix — its leading comments and blank lines — moves onto the table header, and the rest of the key's decor is dropped (which also clears the stray space in `[merge ]`). Both rewrite sites call it, so the migration's `ensure_standard_table_parent` can't drift back.

`values_equal` also gained an `InlineTable` arm. Without it two identical inline tables never compared equal, so a section whose only child is an unchanged inline ta

title: fix(git): protect untracked files hidden by config
body:
## Problem

The destructive clean-worktree guard used bare `git status --porcelain` calls. Git applies the user's `status.showUntrackedFiles` preference to that command, so with:

```ini
[status]
showUntrackedFiles = no
```

a worktree containing only untracked files appeared clean. That false result could let `wt remove`, `wt merge --no-commit`, or unattended `wt step prune` remove the worktree without protecting those files.

The same preference also hid the disclosure printed before `git add -A`: `wt merge`, `wt step commit`, and `wt step squash` still staged and committed the files, but did not name them first.

## Fix

- Make `WorkingTree::is_dirty()` and `dirty_files()` use `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=normal`, overriding the display-only preference for safety checks.
- Make both auto-staging warning queries use `git status --porcelain -z -uall`, so they override the preference and enumerate each file inside untracked directories exactly as `git add -A` will stage it.

## Testing

Regression coverage now exercises:

- Shared clean-check helpers.
- Foreground and background `wt remove`.
- `wt merge --no-commit` before ref changes or cleanup.
- Unattended `wt step prune` while another clean candidate is removed.
- `wt step commit` and `wt step squash` auto-staging warnings with two files inside an untracked directory.

Applying only these tests to the old `origin/main` implementation produced six expected failures across the destructive and disclosure paths. The current branch passes the full project gate:

```text
cargo run -- hook pre-merge --yes
4869 tests passed, 1 skipped
lockfile, pre-commit, clippy, doctest, and rustdoc passed
```

title: fix(switch): name the branch a failed worktree add leaves behind
body:
## Problem

`git worktree add -b <branch>` writes the branch ref before it populates the
worktree, and unwinds only what it registered. A failure in between — an index
git can't write, leading directories it can't create — therefore ends with the
branch present and nothing checked out on it:

```
$ git worktree add -b feat ../blocker/sub master
Preparing worktree (new branch 'feat')
fatal: could not create leading directories of '../blocker/sub/.git': Not a directory
$ git branch
  feat
* master
```

`wt switch --create` reported only `✗ Failed to create worktree for <branch>
from base main`, so the leftover was invisible until the next
`wt switch --create <branch>` answered `Branch <branch> already exists` — which
reads as a fresh name collision rather than as fallout from the first failure.
That second error is what #4108 had to decode.

## Solution

On a failed `--create`, `failed_add_left_branch` asks whether the branch is now
present with no worktree, and `WorktreeCreationFailed` gains a hint naming it
with both recoveries:

```
✗ Failed to create worktree for feature/auth from base main
 ┃ fatal: could not create leading directories
↳ Branch feature/auth was created before the failure, with no worktree; to delete it, run git branch -d -- feature/auth; to use it, run wt switch feature/auth
```

The issue proposed deleting the ref or falling through to the no-create path.
Neither is what this does, and the reasons are worth stating:

- **Deleting it** is the rollback #3984 removed. That rollback's
  did-we-create-it reasoning was wrong once and force-deleted a branch `wt` had
  not created, taking commits only it held. `CLAUDE.md`'s data-safety rule says
  the same thing generally — no implicit destructive side effects, cleanup is a
  separate action the user chooses. A hint costs nothing and leaves the choice
  where it belongs.
- **Falling through** would make `--create` silently adopt an existing branch,
  which hides a genuine name collision — the case the error is for.

The detection is read-only and runs only on the error path. The worktree lookup
goes through a fresh `Repository`, since `repo` cached its inventory before the

title: fix(shell): resolve fish's config directory once, so the wrapper lands where fish reads it
body:
## Problem

`config_paths`'s fish arm resolved the wrapper directory as a hardcoded `~/.config/fish`, while `completion_path`'s fish arm two functions down used the XDG config directory. Same tool, same process, two rules — so a `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` pointing anywhere but `~/.config` sent the two files to different directories. Fish reads `$__fish_config_dir`, which follows `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`: it autoloaded the completion and never saw the wrapper.

Nothing surfaced the split. `wt config shell install fish` printed `✓` for both files, and `wt config show` read its "configured" answer back from the same hardcoded path it had just written, so the report agreed. What the user saw was `wt switch` leaving the shell in the same directory, with completions working.

## Solution

One `fish_config_dir()` helper resolves fish's config directory, and every path fish itself reads goes through it: the wrapper (`config_paths`), the completion (`completion_path`), the directories `wt config shell uninstall` scans, and the `functions/` entry in `scan_for_detection_details` that `wt config show` reports from. Install, uninstall and detection agree on one directory rather than three hardcodes and one lookup.

The helper uses `etcetera`'s `Xdg` strategy rather than `choose_base_strategy`, which resolves `%APPDATA%` on Windows — fish has no `%APPDATA%` notion on any platform, and one resolver with no platform branch is the simpler code. On Unix the two are identical, so this is a no-op there. On Windows it moves the fish completion off `%APPDATA%\fish\completions` onto `%USERPROFILE%\.config\fish\completions`, where the wrapper already resolved — that is the two files agreeing, not a path fish can load: `Xdg::new` takes its home from `std::env::home_dir`, which returns `%USERPROFILE%` on Windows and stopped reading `HOME` there in Rust 1.85, so the POSIX `$HOME` a Cygwin or MSYS fish runs under is the one thing it won't see. The `%APPDATA%` completion an earlier install wrote is left in place, like the other pre-fix files.

Uninstall does not chase the `~/.config/fish` directories a pre-fix install wrote to. Fish never loaded those files, so they are not integration to remove, and scanning a second directory per file kind costs more machinery than the case is worth. The same applies to the Windows completion this moves off `%APPDATA%`.

Two things deliberately stay pinned to `~/.config/fish`:

- `legacy_fish_conf_d_path`, which names a file worktrunk *wrote* rather than one fish reads. Install removes what it resolves to whole and unread, so resolving it through `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` would both stop finding the stranded file and start deleting a `conf.d/{cmd}.fish` in the directory fish actually loads — one worktrunk never wrote. Install's deletion surface is therefore unchanged by this PR.
- `scan_for_detection_details`'s `conf.d` entry, because `config/show.rs` decides `legacy_fish_has_integration` by comparing that result's path against `legacy_fish_conf_d_path`. Resol

title: fix: ignore an empty or relative XDG_*_HOME across every XDG base-directory read
body:
`wt`'s Gitea support reads `tea`'s config file directly to answer "is tea logged in to this host?" — `is_authed_for` for the `wt switch pr:<n>` forge dispatcher, `has_any_login` for the CI-status backend. `read_tea_config` took `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` at face value, so an exported-but-empty value turned the lookup into the relative `tea/config.yml`, resolved against whatever directory `wt` was invoked from. The user's real `~/.config/tea/config.yml` was never read, and where the repository happened to contain a `tea/config.yml`, that file was consulted instead.

With no logins found, both callers report no Gitea login, and the effect is silent:

- `wt list --full` in a Gitea repository drops the CI column (`ci_status/mod.rs` gates the backend on `has_any_login()`).
- `wt switch pr:<n>` against a self-hosted host that `tea` is logged in to falls through to the GitHub CLI (`switch.rs`, the forge dispatcher).

The [XDG base directory spec](https://specifications.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/latest/) makes both exclusions: an unset *or empty* value means the `$HOME`-relative default, and a relative path is invalid and must be ignored.

## Why this isn't gitea-specific

It isn't, and the first revision was wrong to scope it there. worktrunk read an `XDG_*_HOME` variable at four sites, each joining a subpath onto it, and each had written the rule at a different strictness — so `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=cfg` picked the target by cwd at three of them.

The three that mean "the XDG config directory" now delegate to `etcetera::base_strategy::Xdg::config_dir()` — the env read, the spec's absolute-only filter, and the `~/.config` fallback in one call, from the crate worktrunk already resolves its own config with. Each caller's hand-written `~/.config` fallback goes with it, so the fix is net −39 lines.

| Site | Variable | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `read_tea_config` (`git::remote_ref::gitea`) | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | face value | `Xdg::config_dir()` |
| `opencode_plugins_dir` (`commands::config::opencode`) | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | empty filtered, relative not | `Xdg::config_dir()` |
| `legacy_nushell_autoload_dirs` (`shell::paths`) | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | face value | `Xdg::config_dir()` |
| `nushell_data_dir_fallback` (`shell::paths`) | `XDG_DATA_HOME` | absolute-only, written inline | unchanged |

`Xdg` rather than `choose_base_strategy()` at the first three: both tools honor `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` on every platform, which `Xdg` keeps and the native strategies don't. Their *defaults* differ — OpenCode reads `~/.config` everywhere (`~/Library/Application Support/opencode/` is its managed-settings path, which is why `opencode_plugins_dir` already avoided `dirs::config_dir()`), while tea's default comes from `github.com/adrg/xdg`: `~/Library/Application Support` on macOS, `%LOCALAPPDATA%` on Windows. So `Xdg` matches tea's default on Linux only; `choose_base_strategy()` would give `~/Library/Preferences` and `%APPDATA%`, matching it on neither. worktrunk's own config keeps

title: chore: bump jsonschema from 0.53.0 to 0.56.0
body:
Bumps [jsonschema](https://github.com/Stranger6667/jsonschema) from 0.53.0 to 0.56.0.
Release notes

Sourced from jsonschema's releases.

[Python] Release 0.56.0

Added

  • canonical.RawReason, what stopped a run from modeling a document, and RawView.reason and RawView.pointer, carrying it beside the subschema the run stopped on.

Changed

  • Canonicalization of a oneOf whose branches share a region too wide to expand, which spent the document's whole intersection allowance on that choice and kept the document Raw.

Performance

  • Preparing or building a schema that names no base URI parses the default one once for the process instead of once per schema.
  • Canonicalization reads the facets no checker covers once per node instead of once per containment query.

[Ruby] Release 0.56.0

Added

  • JSONSchema::Canonical::RawReason, what stopped a run from modeling a document, and RawView#reason and RawView#pointer, carrying it beside the subschema the run stopped on.

Changed

  • Canonicalization of a oneOf whose branches share a region too wide to expand, which spent the document's whole intersection allowance on that choice and kept the document Raw.

Performance

  • Preparing or building a schema that names no base URI parses the default one once for the process instead of once per schema.
  • Canonicalization reads the facets no checker covers once per node instead of once per containment query.

[Rust] Release 0.56.0

Added

  • canonical::RawReason, what stopped a run from modeling a document, and canonical::RawView, carrying it beside the document and a pointer to the subschema the run stopped on.
  • ValidationOptions::is_known_format, whether a format of that name is checked under a draft.

Changed

  • BREAKING: canonical::CanonicalView::Raw carries a canonical::RawView in place of the document alone.
  • Canonicalization of a oneOf whose branches share a region too wide to expand, which spent the document's whole intersection allowance on that choice and kept the document Raw.

Performance

  • Preparing or building a schema that names no base URI parses the default one once for the process instead of once per schema.
  • Canonicalizing several subschemas of one prepared document compiles each pattern once for the document instead of once per call.
  • Canonicalization reads the facets no checker covers once per node ins

Release notes

Sourced from astral-sh/setup-uv's releases.

v10.1.0 🌈 New output python-runtime-idand respect NO_PROXY

Changes

This release adds more bheind the scene security improvements and also 2 small improvements.

NO_PROXY

This action now respects no_proxy/NO_PROXY environment variables which were previously ignored.

New output python-runtime-id

The new output python-runtime-id can be used to know which python version exactly was installed if you use activate-environment. See pyca/cryptography#15572 for details on why this can be useful.

🐛 Bug fixes

  • fix: respect no proxy directive @​mj0nez (#1037)
  • Use JSON + a typed wrapper instead of TS codegen @​woodruffw (#1025)

title: docs: leave trailing shell comments out of copied commands
body:
Copy buttons copied shell commands with their trailing `#` comments, e.g. `wt hook pre-merge user:        # Run all user hooks`. In zsh without `interactivecomments`, which is the default, a pasted trailing comment isn't a comment: the command runs as `wt hook pre-merge user: '#' Run all user hooks`.

`withoutTrailingShellComments` in `docs/src/plugins/worktrunk-terminal.mjs` applies the shell's rule, that a `#` beginning an unquoted word starts a comment, to what shell copy buttons copy: each per-line button in multi-command `console` blocks, the command lines of single-command `console` blocks, and whole `bash` and `sh` blocks. A line that is only a comment stays, as `docs/CLAUDE.md` already specifies for console blocks. 56 of the site's 339 copy payloads change (47 per-line buttons and 9 `bash` blocks). TOML, PowerShell and other payloads are unchanged, and a quoted `#` survives.

Tests: unit tests for the scanner (quotes, escapes, `$#`, operators, quotes spanning lines) and for a single-command `console` block with a trailing comment, plus a built-site test that no `bash` or `sh` payload carries a trailing comment, which fails on the build before this change.

title: docs: fix misplaced copy buttons by dropping terminal frames
body:
On every shell code block the copy button sat 40px below the top of the code: on the second line of multi-line blocks, and hanging below one-line blocks such as `wt merge --no-ff` on /merge/. Shell blocks were Expressive Code terminal frames, and the terminal plugin deleted their title bar, but Expressive Code still offsets the copy button by that bar's height.

## Changes

- `docs/astro.config.mjs` sets `defaultProps: { frame: 'code' }`, so no block is a terminal frame and there is no title bar to remove. The plugin's header-removal hook and its `props.frame = 'terminal'` go, and so does the `wt-commands-only` class: mobile wrapping in `custom.css` now keys on whether a block contains captured output (`:has(.wt-output)`).
- Blocks with several commands had a whole-block copy button and per-line buttons in the same corner, handed over on hover by opacity. A hidden button still takes clicks, so clicking a line's button could copy the whole block, and on touch screens one button covered another. Most of these blocks are lists of alternatives, so they now get only per-line buttons, and the hover rule is deleted.
- Those blocks wrap (Expressive Code's `wrap` prop) unless they carry captured output, since a per-line button sits at the end of its line and scrolled out of view on the long `jq` examples on /list/. A per-line button is no taller than its line, so buttons on adjacent lines no longer overlap.
- The two multi-command blocks that only work run in order, the FAQ's stash recipe and the `Equivalent to:` block under `wt step diff`'s **How it works** (in `src/cli/step.rs`), are now `bash` fences, the form `docs/CLAUDE.md` prescribes for a copyable recipe, so they keep one copy button for the whole recipe. Terminal `--help` renders `console` and `bash` fences alike (it strips `$ `), and the help snapshots are unchanged.

## Side effect

Expressive Code strips comment lines only from what terminal frames copy. The eight `bash` and `powershell` blocks with comments on /shell-integration/ now copy them, as console blocks already did. Pasted into zsh without `interactivecomments`, each comment line prints `command not found: #`; the commands still run.

## Tests

A browser test checks every copy button on every page, at 393px with touch and at 1376px, for three things: it sits on the line it copies, it is inside the visible code, and it doesn't overlap another button. These checks fail against worktrunk.dev and against a build without the wrap and the height cap. The built-site and plugin tests now expect per-line payloads and no block payload on multi-command blocks, and a plugin test pins that blocks carrying output never wrap.
